items.stem: Enantiopure (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in 80% aqueous ethanol at 50 degrees C and slowly converts to the corresponding alcohol. What stereochemical outcome at the original sp3 carbon is observed in the product mixture?
choices: Racemization producing roughly equal R and S alcohol
Loss of the stereocenter via elimination to an alkene
Formation of a meso diol after a second hydration
items.why: Tertiary substrates in polar protic solvent ionize to a planar sp2 carbocation in the rate-limiting step. Water can then attack from either face with similar probability, giving a near-racemic mixture and net loss of optical activity.

items.stem: 1-Bromobutane is treated with NaCN in DMSO at 25 degrees C. The kinetics are first order in alkyl halide and first order in cyanide. Which description of the rate-limiting step is correct?
choices: Two-step ionization to a primary carbocation, then nucleophile capture
A single concerted bimolecular step with simultaneous bond making and breaking
Reversible carbocation formation followed by loss of a beta proton
Slow deprotonation alpha to the leaving group, then displacement
Pre-equilibrium solvolysis followed by SN1 capture by cyanide
items.why: Second-order kinetics (rate = k[RX][Nu]) signals a one-step concerted SN2 mechanism where the nucleophile attacks at the same time the leaving group departs. No carbocation intermediate forms, especially on primary carbons.

items.stem: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is dissolved in methanol (acting as both solvent and nucleophile) and heated gently. Which mechanism best describes the dominant substitution pathway under these conditions?
choices: SN1, via a tertiary carbocation in protic solvent
SN2, because methanol is a small nucleophile
E2, because methanol acts as a strong base
Radical chain substitution initiated by trace peroxides
items.why: Tertiary substrates cannot undergo backside SN2 attack due to steric crowding. Polar protic solvents stabilize the carbocation and the leaving group, favoring ionization (SN1). Weak nucleophiles like methanol simply trap the cation after it forms.

items.stem: Enantiopure (S)-2-bromobutane reacts with NaSH in acetone at room temperature to give the corresponding thiol. What stereochemical relationship does the product have to the starting material at the reactive carbon?
choices: Inversion of configuration via a Walden-type backside attack
Retention of configuration through a frontside displacement
Racemization through a planar carbocation intermediate
Complete loss of stereochemistry due to elimination
Net retention via a double-inversion neighboring-group pathway
items.why: SN2 on a secondary carbon with a strong nucleophile proceeds by backside attack 180 degrees from the leaving group. The three remaining substituents flip like an umbrella in the wind, giving inversion (Walden inversion) of configuration.

items.stem: 2-Bromopentane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol at 60 degrees C. Which mechanism dominates and what regiochemical outcome is expected for the alkene product?
choices: SN1 ionization followed by tert-butoxide capture
E1 with the more substituted Zaitsev alkene
E2 giving the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene due to the bulky base
Carbocation rearrangement to a tertiary cation, then E1
items.why: Bulky strong bases like t-BuOK cannot easily reach the more hindered internal beta-hydrogen, so they abstract the more accessible terminal beta-hydrogen. This concerted E2 pathway delivers the less substituted Hofmann alkene.

items.stem: Enantiopure (R)-3-iodo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in 75% aqueous acetone and stirred at 40 degrees C. What is the expected stereochemical outcome at the carbon bearing the iodide in the alcohol product?
choices: Approximately 50/50 R and S product (racemic mixture)
No change because the C-I bond does not break
items.why: Tertiary substrates ionize in polar protic solvent to a planar carbocation. Solvent then attacks both faces with nearly equal probability, scrambling stereochemistry and producing a racemic SN1 alcohol mixture.

items.stem: tert-Butyl chloride is heated in 80% aqueous ethanol with no added strong base or strong nucleophile. Which mechanism best accounts for the formation of tert-butyl alcohol under these conditions?
choices: SN1, via a tertiary carbocation stabilized by the protic solvent
SN2, with concerted backside attack by water
E2, with ethanol acting as a strong base
items.why: Tertiary halides in polar protic solvents lose the leaving group to form a stabilized 3 degrees carbocation in the rate-limiting step. The weak nucleophile (water/ethanol) then captures the cation, giving SN1 substitution.

items.stem: 2-Iodo-2-methylpropane is stirred in pure methanol at 45 degrees C with no added base. Methyl tert-butyl ether forms slowly. Which mechanism best explains this transformation?
choices: Concerted SN2 backside attack by methanol
Stepwise SN1 ionization to a 3 degrees carbocation captured by methanol
E2 with methanol as a base, followed by re-addition
Carbene insertion of methylene into a C-O bond
items.why: Tertiary alkyl halides cannot undergo SN2 because of steric blocking of the backside. Polar protic methanol stabilizes the resulting tertiary carbocation; methanol then acts as a weak nucleophile to give SN1 product (the ether).

items.stem: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated in pure ethanol at 70 degrees C with no added base. The product mixture contains alkenes and an ethyl ether in roughly comparable amounts. Which set of mechanisms best accounts for these products?
choices: E1 producing alkenes, alongside SN1 forming the ethyl ether
SN2 only, giving the ethyl ether exclusively
E2 only, giving Zaitsev alkene exclusively
SN1 only, giving the ethyl ether exclusively
items.why: Tertiary substrates in hot polar protic solvent generate a carbocation in the rate-limiting step. From there, loss of a beta-proton (E1) competes with capture by ethanol (SN1), so both elimination and substitution products form together.

items.stem: Two elimination experiments on 2-bromobutane are run: one with concentrated NaOEt in ethanol, and one in aqueous acetone with no added base. Which mechanism's experimentally measured rate law contains the base concentration?
choices: Both E1 and E2 contain [base] in their rate laws
E1, because the carbocation must be deprotonated by base
E2, since base removes the beta-H in the slow step
Neither, because elimination is always solvent-driven
Only the competing SN2 pathway includes the base
items.why: E2 is concerted and bimolecular, so the rate equals k[RX][base]. E1 has a slow ionization step that does not involve base; the base is consumed only after the rate-limiting step, so it does not appear in the rate law.

items.stem: A student measures the rate of a beta-elimination of 2-chloro-2-methylpentane and finds rate = k[RX][NaOEt]. Which elimination mechanism is consistent with this rate expression?
items.why: A second-order rate law with both substrate and base implies a concerted, bimolecular transition state where C-H and C-X break while pi bond forms. That is the defining feature of E2.

items.stem: Solvolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane in 80% aqueous acetone follows the rate law rate = k[RX] with no [Nu] dependence. Which step is rate-limiting in this SN1 process?
choices: Ionization of the C-X bond to form a carbocation and free leaving group
Attack of water on the substrate before ionization
Loss of a beta-hydrogen from the cation
A single concerted step involving both substrate and nucleophile
Reversible protonation of the leaving group
items.why: An SN1 reaction's slow step is unimolecular C-X heterolysis, generating the carbocation. Because the nucleophile reacts only after this step, [Nu] does not appear in the rate law.

items.stem: (S)-2-bromooctane reacts with NaN3 in DMSO. Doubling either the alkyl halide concentration or the azide concentration doubles the rate. Which step is rate-limiting?
choices: Ionization of the C-Br bond to an octyl carbocation
Loss of a beta-H to give an alkene, then azide addition
Formation of a contact ion pair in a pre-equilibrium
Radical abstraction of bromine before substitution
One concerted step: azide attacks as bromide leaves
items.why: When the rate depends on both [substrate] and [nucleophile], the mechanism is bimolecular and concerted. SN2 has a single transition state in which bond-making and bond-breaking happen simultaneously.

items.stem: tert-Amyl bromide (2-bromo-2-methylbutane) is refluxed in ethanol for several hours with no added base. The product mixture contains 2-methyl-2-butene, 2-methyl-1-butene, and tert-amyl ethyl ether. Which mechanistic combination is responsible?
choices: SN2 only on a tertiary substrate
Pure E2 with ethanol as the base
items.why: Heating a tertiary alkyl halide in a polar protic solvent without strong base favors ionization. The resulting tertiary cation is partitioned between loss of a beta-H (E1, giving alkenes) and ethanol capture (SN1, giving ether).

items.stem: A kinetic study of dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromobutane with NaOMe in MeOH reveals rate = k[2-bromobutane][NaOMe]. Which elimination mechanism includes base in its rate-determining step?
choices: Neither E1 nor E2 has base in the rate law
E1, because base attacks the carbocation
E2, as base removes beta-H in the slow step
Both E1 and E2 have base in their rate laws
Only E1cb mechanisms show this dependence
items.why: Bimolecular kinetics imply a concerted single-step transition state involving both substrate and base. That is E2: removal of the beta-H, formation of the pi bond, and loss of the leaving group all occur together.

items.stem: Solvolysis of 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane in 70% aqueous acetone displays a rate law independent of nucleophile concentration. Which step is rate-determining for this SN1 pathway?
choices: Loss of an alpha-H to form a carbene
Heterolysis of the C-Br bond to form a tertiary carbocation
Initial protonation of the bromide leaving group
items.why: If [Nu] does not influence rate, then the nucleophile is not present in the slow step. Tertiary substrates ionize first to a stable 3 degrees carbocation; the nucleophile only traps it afterward.

items.stem: 3-Iodo-3-ethylpentane (a fully tertiary alkyl iodide) is stirred in 90% aqueous methanol at 40 degrees C with no added base. Which substitution mechanism produces the observed methyl ether?
choices: E2 followed by re-addition of methanol
SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation
SN2 by backside attack of methanol
items.why: Tertiary carbons block SN2 attack sterically. In a polar protic solvent, the C-I bond ionizes; the planar carbocation is then trapped by the weak nucleophile methanol, giving the SN1 ether.

items.stem: 2-Chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane is dissolved in 80% aqueous ethanol at 50 degrees C with no added base. The rate does not depend on any added nucleophile, and the tertiary alcohol and ether are formed along with some alkene. Which mechanism best explains the substitution products?
choices: SN2, in which no rearrangement is possible
E2, removing the bulky internal proton
items.why: A tertiary chloride in a polar protic solvent with no strong nucleophile ionizes first: the slow step is loss of chloride to give the tertiary carbocation, and water or ethanol then traps it. Rate independent of nucleophile is the SN1 signature; SN2 cannot occur at a crowded tertiary carbon.

items.stem: Optically active (R)-3-bromo-3-phenylhexane undergoes solvolysis in 80% aqueous acetone. The product 3-phenylhexan-3-ol shows essentially no optical rotation. What stereochemical outcome does this indicate at the original sp3 carbon?
choices: Net retention through a tight ion pair
No change because the C-Br bond does not break
Racemization through a planar benzylic carbocation
items.why: Loss of optical activity is a hallmark of SN1. The substrate ionizes to a flat sp2 cation (here, benzylic and tertiary), so the nucleophile attacks both faces with similar probability and yields a racemic alcohol.

items.stem: When 2-bromopentane is treated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, kinetic measurements give rate = k[2-bromopentane][NaOEt]. In which elimination mechanism does the base concentration appear in the rate law?
choices: E2, because base removes the beta-H in a concerted step
Only Hofmann elimination of ammonium salts
items.why: E2 requires the base to deprotonate the beta-carbon in the same step as C-X bond cleavage. That makes it bimolecular. E1's slow step is loss of the leaving group alone, so base does not enter the rate law.

items.stem: An SN1 reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane in 80% aqueous ethanol shows first-order kinetics in the substrate and zero-order dependence on water. Which step is rate-limiting?
choices: Attack of water on the tertiary carbocation
Ionization of C-Br to a tertiary carbocation
Loss of a beta-H from the alkyl halide by water
Methyl migration to form a more stable cation
items.why: First-order kinetics with no nucleophile dependence and observable rearrangement both diagnose carbocation formation as the slow step. After ionization, rearrangement and trapping by water occur in fast subsequent steps.

items.stem: 1-Iodopentane reacts with 1.0 M NaCN in DMSO at 25 degrees C to produce hexanenitrile cleanly. Doubling either reactant doubles the rate. Which mechanism is operating, and why?
choices: SN1: a primary carbocation is uniquely stable in polar aprotic DMSO
E2: cyanide acts as a base and removes the beta-hydrogen
E1: ionization to a cation precedes loss of a beta proton
SN2: primary halide, strong nucleophile, second-order rate
Radical chain substitution, initiated and catalyzed by light
items.why: Primary alkyl halides don't form stable cations, so SN1/E1 are not viable. A strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent (which de-shields the nucleophile) and bimolecular kinetics are textbook SN2 conditions.

items.stem: (S)-2-Bromopentane is heated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol at 60 degrees C. The major product is the less substituted alkene 1-pentene rather than 2-pentene. Which mechanism is responsible?
choices: SN2 displacement of bromide by tert-butoxide
SN1 ionization, with later isomerization of the alkene
E2 to the Hofmann alkene, steered by the bulky base
E1 favoring the Zaitsev alkene through cation intermediacy
items.why: Bulky bases like t-BuOK can't fit at the more crowded internal beta-H, so they remove the more accessible terminal beta-H. The result is concerted bimolecular E2 that disobeys Zaitsev and gives the Hofmann alkene.

items.stem: Solvolysis of 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane in 80% aqueous acetone follows rate = k[RX] with rearranged product detected. Which step controls the rate of this SN1 process?
choices: Ionization of the C-Cl bond to a 3° carbocation
Backside attack of water on the alkyl halide
Concerted loss of HCl across the C-C bond
Capture of the carbocation by water as nucleophile
Migration of a methyl group across the C-C bond
items.why: Independence of rate from nucleophile concentration, plus carbocation rearrangement, points to ionization as the slow step. Once the cation forms, rearrangement and trapping happen quickly in non-rate-determining steps.

items.stem: 2-Iodopentane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in t-BuOH at 65 degrees C. The major alkene is 1-pentene rather than 2-pentene. Which mechanism best explains this regiochemical outcome?
choices: E2 giving the Hofmann product, steered by the bulky base
SN2 substitution by tert-butoxide, with retention
E1 favoring the Zaitsev product through a secondary carbocation
SN1 ionization with later proton loss to the more substituted face
Radical chain elimination initiated by heat
items.why: Bulky strong bases force the elimination toward the less hindered beta-hydrogen, giving the less substituted Hofmann alkene. The reaction is concerted (E2) because the base is strong and the substrate is secondary.

items.stem: Enantiopure (R)-2-iodobutane reacts with NaSCH3 in DMSO at 30 degrees C. The product is the corresponding sulfide with a measured optical rotation opposite in sign to the starting material. What stereochemical outcome at the reactive carbon explains this?
choices: Racemization through a flat carbocation intermediate
Walden inversion via concerted backside SN2 attack
No change in configuration; the sign change is solvent-induced
Retention of configuration via a frontside displacement
items.why: A strong nucleophile, a polar aprotic solvent, and a secondary substrate favor SN2. The nucleophile attacks 180 degrees from the leaving group, inverting all three remaining substituents (Walden inversion) and flipping the sign of rotation.

items.stem: tert-Amyl chloride (2-chloro-2-methylbutane) is refluxed in ethanol for 12 hours with no added base. GC analysis shows mostly 2-methyl-2-butene plus minor 2-methyl-1-butene, along with some tert-amyl ethyl ether. Which mechanistic combination dominates?
choices: SN2 by ethanol on a tertiary carbon
E2 only, with ethanol acting as a strong base
Pure SN1, with no alkene formed at all
items.why: Tertiary substrates in hot polar protic solvents ionize to a carbocation. From the cation, loss of a beta-H gives alkenes (E1, with Zaitsev preference) while solvent capture gives an ether (SN1). The product distribution is the classic E1/SN1 fingerprint.

items.stem: Enantiopure (R)-2-bromooctane reacts with NaN3 (strong nucleophile) in dry DMF at 25 degrees C, giving (S)-2-azidooctane with high enantiomeric excess. What stereochemical outcome at the reactive carbon does this confirm?
choices: Racemization through a planar secondary carbocation
Retention of configuration via frontside attack
No change because the C-Br bond does not cleave
Walden inversion through concerted backside SN2
items.why: Polar aprotic DMF de-shields the nucleophile, accelerating SN2 attack on a secondary carbon. Backside attack of azide rotates the three remaining substituents 180 degrees, inverting absolute configuration (R becomes S).

items.stem: (R)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in 90% aqueous acetone at 35 degrees C. The alcohol product shows no measurable optical rotation despite starting from a single enantiomer. What stereochemical outcome explains the result?
choices: Racemization via a planar, achiral carbocation
Pure inversion to (S) via backside SN2
Loss of the stereocenter through alkene formation
A meso diastereomer with an internal mirror plane
items.why: Tertiary substrates ionize to a carbocation in polar protic solvent. The cation is flat (sp2), so water attacks both faces about equally, giving a 1:1 mixture of R and S alcohol that is optically inactive (racemic SN1 product).

items.stem: (S)-2-iodooctane reacts with sodium iodide labeled with radioactive 131-I in dry acetone. The reaction follows second-order kinetics, and the product racemizes at twice the rate it incorporates 131-I. What stereochemical event explains the rate ratio?
choices: SN1 ionization with loss of stereochemistry
Each SN2 event with iodide inverts the carbon, so two displacements (one to S, one back to R) appear as one racemization event
Retention via a tight ion pair
items.why: Each backside SN2 attack by I- inverts configuration (Walden inversion). Two successive inversions return the molecule to the original configuration, so the molecule must invert twice to look 'racemized' once, giving the observed 2:1 ratio.

items.stem: Consider (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane. Although it has two stereocenters, it possesses an internal mirror plane that relates one half of the molecule to the other. What classification best describes this molecule?
items.why: A molecule with chirality centers but an internal plane of symmetry is superimposable on its mirror image and is therefore achiral overall. This is the definition of a meso compound.

items.stem: When assigning configuration at a stereocenter, the lowest-priority substituent is oriented toward the viewer (a 'wedge in') and the visible 1->2->3 priority arc traces clockwise. What is the true configuration?
choices: R, taking the apparent rotation as drawn
S, since the apparent direction is reversed
Achiral; no configuration can be assigned
Meso, because the lowest priority is in front
E or Z, as for an alkene double bond
items.why: CIP rules require viewing the stereocenter with the lowest-priority group pointing away. When it points toward you, the apparent rotation is reversed. Apparent clockwise therefore corresponds to true counterclockwise (S).

items.stem: A compound has two stereocenters and is found to contain an internal mirror plane that interconverts the two halves. The molecule does not rotate plane-polarized light. Which classification fits?
choices: An enantiomer of an unrelated chiral isomer
items.why: Meso compounds contain stereocenters but also a symmetry element (typically a mirror plane) that makes them superimposable on their mirror images. The internal symmetry cancels their optical activity.

items.stem: At a stereocenter, four substituents are -OH, -NH2, -CH3, and -H. Using Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules based on atomic number at the first point of difference, what is the correct priority order from highest to lowest?
items.why: CIP priority at the first atom is by atomic number: O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1). So -OH outranks -NH2, which outranks -CH3, which outranks -H.

items.stem: Tartaric acid in its (2R,3S) form has two stereocenters connected by an internal mirror plane that exchanges them. What stereochemical category describes this isomer of tartaric acid?
choices: A racemic mixture of two enantiomers
A geometric (E/Z) isomer of the acid
items.why: An internal mirror plane between two stereocenters relates the halves and makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image. That is a meso compound; (2R,3S)-tartaric acid is the textbook example.

items.stem: At a stereocenter, the lowest-priority substituent points away from the viewer. The 1->2->3 priority arc, viewed from the opposite side, sweeps clockwise. What is the configuration?
items.why: When the lowest-priority group is oriented away, the visible 1->2->3 rotation is read directly. Clockwise corresponds to R; counterclockwise would be S.

items.stem: Consider (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane. Each carbon bears H, CH3, Br, and a different second carbon, so each is a CIP stereocenter. How many stereocenters does the molecule have?
items.why: Carbons 2 and 3 each carry four different substituents (H, CH3, Br, and a different remaining group), so they are independent stereocenters. The molecule has two even though it is meso.

items.stem: (2R,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane is symmetric: each end of the molecule mirrors the other through a plane perpendicular to the C2-C3 bond. The compound is optically inactive in the pure state. Which classification fits?
choices: A racemic mixture of two enantiomers
A pair of enantiomers in dynamic equilibrium
items.why: Two stereocenters with an internal mirror plane create a molecule that is superimposable on its mirror image. Such molecules are meso and are intrinsically achiral, even as a single, pure compound.

items.stem: How many CIP stereocenters are present in (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane, considering each carbon's substituents (H, CH3, Br, and the rest of the chain)?
items.why: Carbons 2 and 3 each have four distinct substituents and are stereocenters. The molecule has 2 stereocenters; despite being meso overall, each carbon still possesses stereogenic character.

items.stem: While assigning a stereocenter on paper, a student notices that the lowest-priority group is drawn on a wedge coming out toward them. The visible 1->2->3 priority arc rotates clockwise. What is the actual configuration?
choices: S, since the apparent sense is reversed
Meso, by the internal symmetry rule
Cannot be determined without a 3D model
items.why: CIP requires viewing with the lowest priority pointing away. When it points toward you, you see the 'wrong' side, so apparent clockwise rotation is really counterclockwise. The configuration is therefore S.

items.stem: A drawing shows a stereocenter where the lowest-priority H points toward the viewer (a wedge) and the remaining 1->2->3 priorities trace clockwise. What is the actual CIP configuration?
choices: S, because the apparent direction must be inverted when lowest priority points toward you
R, taken directly from the drawing
Both R and S are possible
items.why: When the lowest priority is on a wedge (toward you), the apparent rotation must be reversed. A clockwise sweep as drawn corresponds to a true counterclockwise sweep, which is S.

items.stem: (2R,3S)-Tartaric acid contains two stereocenters but possesses an internal mirror plane between C2 and C3. Pure samples do not rotate polarized light. Which stereochemical classification applies?
choices: A diastereomer of (2R,3S) without any symmetry
items.why: An internal mirror plane between the two stereocenters makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image. It is achiral despite containing chirality centers, which is the definition of a meso compound.

items.stem: A textbook drawing places the lowest-priority substituent on a wedge pointing toward the viewer at a stereocenter. The remaining priorities 1->2->3 are arranged clockwise. What is the actual configuration?
choices: S, since viewing from the front reverses the apparent direction
items.why: CIP requires viewing with the lowest-priority group away from the viewer. With it pointing toward the viewer, the rotation reads backward, so apparent clockwise (which would be R) is really S.

items.stem: At a stereocenter, the lowest-priority substituent points directly away from the viewer (on a dashed bond). The visible 1->2->3 sweep is clockwise. What is the configuration?
items.why: With the lowest priority pointing away, the visible rotation is read directly. Clockwise corresponds to R (rectus). Counterclockwise would be S.

items.stem: At a stereocenter the lowest-priority group lies on a dashed bond pointing into the page. The visible 1->2->3 priorities trace counterclockwise. What is the CIP configuration?
items.why: When the lowest priority is oriented away from the viewer, the visible rotation is the actual configuration. Counterclockwise (left-turning, sinister) corresponds to S.

items.stem: (2R,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane contains two stereocenters but is internally symmetric: a mirror plane runs perpendicular to the C2-C3 bond. The neat liquid has zero optical rotation. Which stereochemical descriptor fits?
items.why: An internal plane of symmetry makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image; the optical rotations from each chiral half cancel. Such a single stereoisomer with no net chirality is a meso compound.

items.stem: At a stereocenter the lowest-priority H is drawn on a dashed bond going into the page. The visible 1->2->3 priorities sweep clockwise around the carbon. What is the CIP configuration?
choices: Cannot be assigned without IR data
items.why: When the lowest-priority substituent points away, the visible rotation around the remaining three groups is read directly. A clockwise (rectus) sweep is R.

items.stem: (2R,3S)-Tartaric acid contains two stereocenters yet does not rotate polarized light because an internal mirror plane bisects the molecule. Which stereochemical category applies?
items.why: Meso compounds have stereocenters but also possess an internal mirror plane (or other improper symmetry element) that makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image. The two halves' rotations cancel.

items.stem: A student examines a Fischer-style drawing where the lowest-priority H sits on a wedge pointing toward them. The 1->2->3 CIP priorities sweep clockwise. What is the actual configuration of the stereocenter?
choices: R, read directly from the drawing as shown
S, since the H points toward the viewer
Meso, with an internal mirror plane
items.why: When the lowest-priority group is on a wedge pointing toward you, the visible direction of rotation is opposite the true direction. Apparent clockwise therefore corresponds to true counterclockwise (S).

items.stem: At a single stereocenter, the four substituents are -OH, -NH2, -CH3, and -H. Using Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules and atomic number at the first point of difference, what is the priority order from highest to lowest?
items.why: First-atom priorities go by atomic number: O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1). So -OH is highest, then -NH2, then -CH3, then -H. The order does not depend on what is further down the chain when the first atoms already differ.

items.stem: (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane has each interior carbon bonded to H, CH3, Br, and a distinct remaining group. How many CIP stereocenters does this meso molecule formally contain?
items.why: Both C2 and C3 bear four different substituents (H, CH3, Br, and a different remainder of the chain), so each is a stereocenter. Two stereocenters can still be 'meso' if there is an internal mirror plane.

items.stem: A compound contains exactly two stereocenters and an internal mirror plane that exchanges them. The pure compound is optically inactive at all wavelengths. Which stereochemical classification fits this description?
items.why: An internal mirror plane between two stereocenters generates a molecule that is superimposable on its mirror image. Such a molecule is achiral despite having chirality centers, which is the definition of a meso compound.

items.stem: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, then a reductive workup with Zn in aqueous acetic acid. What is the expected major product after this two-step ozonolysis sequence?
items.why: Ozone cleaves the C=C bond to form an ozonide. Reductive workup (Zn/AcOH) yields aldehydes from each carbon of the original double bond. Cleaving cyclohexene's ring opens the chain into the dialdehyde hexanedial.

items.stem: Propene is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 at 25 degrees C with no peroxides present. Following Markovnikov's rule, which alcohol forms as the major product?
items.why: Acid-catalyzed hydration adds H+ first to give the more stable carbocation; here, the secondary cation forms at C2. Water then adds at C2, and deprotonation gives 2-propanol. This is a textbook Markovnikov addition.

items.stem: Propene is treated with 1 equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark. Which product, and with what stereochemistry where applicable, is expected?
choices: 1,2-Dibromopropane via anti addition through a bromonium ion intermediate
items.why: Br2 forms a cyclic bromonium ion across the double bond; bromide attacks the back face, giving anti addition. The product on propene is 1,2-dibromopropane. Light-free, halogenated solvents prevent radical allylic bromination.

items.stem: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxides (e.g., ROOR) under radical conditions. Which alkyl bromide forms as the major product?
items.why: Peroxides switch the mechanism to a radical chain: Br radical adds first to the less substituted carbon to give the more stable secondary radical. H then caps the more substituted carbon, placing Br at C1. The result is anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropane.

items.stem: Propene is bubbled through anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C in the absence of peroxides or light. What is the major product following Markovnikov's rule?
items.why: Without peroxides, ionic addition prevails. H+ adds first to give the more stable secondary carbocation at C2; Br- then attacks to give 2-bromopropane, the Markovnikov product.

items.stem: Propene is treated with BH3 in THF at 0 degrees C, then oxidatively worked up with H2O2 and aqueous NaOH. What major alcohol forms, and what is its regiochemistry relative to the starting alkene?
choices: 1-Propanol; anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH
items.why: Hydroboration delivers BH3 with boron on the less hindered carbon (anti-Markovnikov) and adds H/B syn across the alkene. Oxidation with basic peroxide replaces B with OH with retention, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-propanol.

items.stem: Propene is treated with cold, dilute, basic aqueous KMnO4. What is the major product of this oxidative addition?
items.why: Cold, dilute KMnO4 performs syn dihydroxylation across the double bond by way of a cyclic manganate ester. The two new OH groups are added on the same face. With propene, the product is 1,2-propanediol.

items.stem: Propene is reacted with anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C in the absence of peroxides. What is the major product of this ionic addition, and what regiochemical rule controls the outcome?
items.why: Ionic addition adds H+ first to form the more stable carbocation, and the secondary cation is favored over the primary one. Br- then traps the cation at C2, giving 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov product).

items.stem: Propene is treated with cold dilute KMnO4 in basic aqueous solution. The reaction is kept ice-cold to avoid over-oxidation. What is the major product?
items.why: Cold, dilute KMnO4 in base performs syn dihydroxylation across the double bond via a cyclic manganate intermediate. Both OH groups add to the same face, giving 1,2-propanediol from propene.

items.stem: Propene reacts with anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C with no peroxides. Identify the major product and explain which regiochemistry rule applies.
choices: 2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov), through the more stable secondary carbocation
items.why: Ionic HBr addition proceeds through the more stable carbocation, which is secondary (at C2). Bromide adds to that cation to give 2-bromopropane. With no peroxides, the radical pathway is shut off and Markovnikov dominates.

items.stem: Propene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark. What product and stereochemistry are expected from this electrophilic addition?
choices: 1,2-Dibromopropane via anti addition through a bromonium ion
items.why: Br2 forms a cyclic bromonium ion across the alkene. Bromide attacks the back face, opening the ring, so addition is anti (trans). On propene, this places Br on adjacent carbons to give 1,2-dibromopropane.

items.stem: Propene is treated with BH3 in THF at 0 degrees C, then with H2O2 and aqueous NaOH. Predict the major product, including its regiochemistry relative to the original double bond.
items.why: Hydroboration places boron on the less hindered (terminal) carbon with syn delivery of B and H. Oxidative workup converts B to OH with retention of configuration, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-propanol.

items.stem: Propene is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 at 25 degrees C without peroxides. Which alcohol is the Markovnikov product, and what cation intermediate explains the regioselectivity?
choices: Propanal, via oxidation of the alkene
Propane, via net addition of H2
items.why: Acid-catalyzed hydration protonates the alkene to give the more stable carbocation; the secondary cation at C2 is favored over the primary at C1. Water traps it and deprotonation gives 2-propanol.

items.stem: Propene is treated with cold, dilute, basic KMnO4 (the so-called Baeyer test conditions). What is the major product, and what stereochemistry does the addition follow?
items.why: Cold, dilute, basic KMnO4 forms a cyclic manganate ester across the alkene, then hydrolyzes to deliver two OH groups on the same face. The product on propene is 1,2-propanediol with syn stereochemistry.

items.stem: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, then Zn/AcOH. What major product forms after this reductive ozonolysis?
items.why: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond. Reductive workup (Zn/AcOH) stops oxidation at the aldehyde stage. Cleaving the ring of cyclohexene opens it into the linear dialdehyde hexanedial.

items.stem: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, followed by Zn/H2O. Which product results from this reductive ozonolysis?
items.why: Reductive workup of the ozonide preserves both new C=O bonds at the aldehyde oxidation level. Because cyclohexene's C=C is part of a ring, cleavage opens the ring into a single chain with aldehydes at each end (hexanedial).

items.stem: Propene is hydrogenated with H2 (1 atm) over a Pd/C catalyst in ethanol at 25 degrees C. What is the product of this catalytic hydrogenation?
items.why: Pd/C with H2 performs syn addition of two H atoms across the C=C bond. With propene, both faces of the double bond accept hydrogen and the product is propane.

items.stem: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of dibenzoyl peroxide (a radical initiator). Which product is favored under these radical conditions?
items.why: Peroxides initiate a radical chain in which Br* adds first to the less substituted carbon to form the more stable secondary radical. H* then caps the more substituted carbon, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropane.

items.stem: Propene is treated with cold, dilute KMnO4 in basic aqueous solution at 0 degrees C. Which product, with which stereochemistry, results from this Baeyer test?
choices: Propanoic acid, via oxidative C=C cleavage
Propane, via reduction of the alkene
items.why: Cold, dilute KMnO4 forms a cyclic Mn(V) ester across the alkene. Hydrolysis gives a syn diol because both OH groups end up on the same face. With propene, the product is 1,2-propanediol.

items.stem: Propene undergoes hydroboration with BH3 in THF at 0 degrees C, followed by basic peroxide workup (H2O2, NaOH). What is the major product, and what is the regio/stereochemistry of the overall transformation?
items.why: Hydroboration adds H and B across the alkene in a concerted, syn fashion with B on the less hindered carbon (anti-Markovnikov). Basic peroxide oxidation replaces C-B with C-OH stereospecifically, giving 1-propanol.

items.stem: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, then with Zn/AcOH workup. Identify the major product and explain why a ring-opened compound forms instead of a cyclic ketone.
choices: Hexanedial, as ozonolysis opens the ring
items.why: Ozone breaks the C=C bond and reductive workup gives carbonyls at the aldehyde stage. Because cyclohexene's double bond is part of the ring, cleaving it converts a cyclic alkene into an open dialdehyde chain (hexanedial).

items.stem: Propene is treated with Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C, kept in the dark to suppress radicals. What is the major product, and what stereochemistry does it inherit from the bromonium ion intermediate?
items.why: Br2 forms a bridged bromonium ion across the C=C; bromide opens it from the back face, so the two Br atoms add anti (trans). On propene this gives vicinal 1,2-dibromopropane.

items.stem: Propene reacts with anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C in the dark with no peroxides. Why does the Markovnikov product dominate, and what is it?
choices: Propene recovered; HBr does not add in the dark
Propane; HBr transfers H2 to the alkene
items.why: Without peroxides, addition is ionic. Protonation gives the more stable carbocation, and a secondary cation is favored over a primary one. Bromide then captures the secondary cation to form 2-bromopropane.

items.stem: Treating propene with one equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark gives anti addition. Identify the major product and explain the stereochemical outcome.
choices: 1,1-Dibromopropane, a geminal dibromide on one carbon
Propylene oxide, formed by ring closure
items.why: Br2 first forms a cyclic bromonium ion, then bromide attacks from the opposite face. The result is a vicinal dibromide with anti stereochemistry. On propene, this is 1,2-dibromopropane.

items.stem: Propene is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 at 25 degrees C with no peroxides. Predict the major alcohol and explain why a primary product is not favored.
choices: 1-Propanol; primary cations are stabilized by hyperconjugation
Propanal via oxidation of the alkene
2-Propanol (Markovnikov); the secondary carbocation at C2 is more stable than the primary at C1
items.why: Acid-catalyzed hydration protonates the alkene to give the more stable carbocation. A secondary cation at C2 is much more stable than a primary cation at C1, so water adds at C2 to give 2-propanol.

items.stem: Cyclohexene is exposed to O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C and then worked up with Zn/AcOH (reductive conditions). Predict the major product and contrast it with what would form under oxidative workup.
choices: Cyclohexanone, since the ring is preserved
Hexanedioic acid (adipic acid), the oxidative-workup product
Hexanedial, from reductive workup of the ozonide
Cyclohexanol from reduction of the alkene
items.why: Ozone cleaves the cyclic C=C and the ozonide is reduced by Zn/AcOH to two aldehydes, opening the ring into hexanedial. Oxidative workup (H2O2) would push the aldehydes to carboxylic acids (adipic acid).

items.stem: Propene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark. What is the major product, and what mechanistic feature controls the stereochemistry?
choices: 1,2-Dibromopropane via anti opening of a bridged bromonium ion
items.why: Halogenation of an alkene proceeds through a cyclic halonium ion that is opened by the second halide on the opposite face. On propene, this generates the vicinal anti dibromide 1,2-dibromopropane.

items.stem: Propene is treated with HBr in the presence of dibenzoyl peroxide at 80 degrees C. What is the major product, and which intermediate explains its anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry?
choices: 1-Bromopropane; the secondary radical formed by Br* addition to C1 is more stable than the primary one
items.why: With peroxides, HBr adds by a radical chain. Br* adds to the less substituted carbon (C1) to give the more stable secondary carbon radical at C2; H* then adds at C2. The Br ends up at C1, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropane.

items.stem: 2-Butyne is hydrogenated with H2 over a Lindlar catalyst (Pd/CaCO3 poisoned with Pb, in quinoline). What is the major product and its geometry?
choices: cis-2-butene from syn addition stopped at the alkene
items.why: Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned Pd that adds H2 only once and only on the same face. Both H atoms add syn to the same side of the alkyne, locking the alkene as cis (Z). 2-Butyne becomes cis-2-butene.

items.stem: 1-Butyne is treated with NaNH2 in liquid NH3 at -33 degrees C. What is the major species formed, and which proton is removed?
choices: No reaction; sp3 C-H bonds are too weak to abstract
The acetylide anion via deprotonation of the terminal sp C-H (pKa ~25)
A carbanion at C4 via Sigma-bond metathesis
items.why: Terminal alkyne C-H bonds have pKa ~25, much more acidic than vinyl or allyl C-H bonds because the conjugate base sits in an sp orbital with high s character. NaNH2 (pKa of NH3 ~38) is strong enough to deprotonate to give the acetylide.

items.stem: 1-Butyne reacts with NaNH2 in liquid ammonia. What product results from this acid-base reaction at the terminal carbon?
choices: No reaction because C-H bonds do not ionize
Vinyl anion from a CH=CH-CH3 fragment
items.why: Terminal alkynes are weak acids (pKa ~25) because the sp-hybridized C-H places the lone pair in a high-s-character orbital. NaNH2 (conjugate acid pKa ~38) removes the terminal H to give the acetylide nucleophile.

items.stem: 1-Butyne is added to NaNH2 in liquid ammonia (-33 degrees C). What is the immediate organic product of this acid-base reaction?
choices: No reaction because alkynes are not acidic enough
items.why: Terminal alkynes have a relatively acidic sp C-H (pKa ~25). Sodium amide (pKa of conjugate acid ~38) is a strong enough base to deprotonate them, generating an sp-hybridized acetylide carbanion.

items.stem: 1-Butyne is treated with NaNH2 in liquid NH3 at -33 degrees C. Which species forms after the acid-base step?
choices: A vinyl anion at the internal carbon
No reaction; bonds are too strong
items.why: Acetylene C-H bonds (pKa ~25) are more acidic than vinyl (pKa ~44) or alkyl (pKa ~50) bonds because the lone pair on the conjugate base resides in an sp orbital. Sodium amide easily abstracts that proton to give the acetylide.

items.stem: 1-Butyne is added to a solution of NaNH2 in liquid NH3 to form a nucleophile that is later alkylated. What species does this acid-base step generate?
choices: A vinyl anion via deprotonation at sp2 carbon
The terminal acetylide anion via deprotonation at sp carbon
No reaction; pKa is too high
items.why: Acetylenic C-H bonds are unusually acidic (pKa ~25) because the sp orbital holding the lone pair has 50% s character, stabilizing the negative charge. NaNH2 readily removes that H to generate the acetylide nucleophile.

items.stem: Treating 1-butyne with NaNH2 in liquid ammonia is a standard preparation for which intermediate used in alkylations and cuprate chemistry?
choices: A vinyl anion at the internal alkyne carbon
items.why: Terminal alkynes have an acidic sp C-H (pKa ~25). NaNH2 (pKa ~38) deprotonates it cleanly to give the sodium acetylide, a key nucleophile for SN2 alkylations and metal-mediated cross-couplings.

items.stem: 2-Butyne is treated with sodium metal dissolved in liquid ammonia at -33 degrees C (a 'dissolving metal' reduction). What major product, and with what alkene geometry, is formed?
choices: trans-2-butene from anti addition through a vinyl radical/anion intermediate
items.why: Na/NH3 reduces alkynes by sequential single-electron transfers and protonations. The vinyl radical and anion adopt the more stable trans (E) geometry before the second protonation, locking in the trans alkene.

items.stem: Acetylene (HC#CH) is treated with 2 equivalents of HBr in CH2Cl2 at 0 degC in the absence of peroxides. What is the major organic product after both additions are complete?
items.why: HBr adds to alkynes by Markovnikov regiochemistry in the absence of peroxides: the first equivalent gives vinyl bromide (CH2=CHBr). The second HBr addition is again Markovnikov because the Br on the alkene stabilizes the adjacent carbocation through lone-pair donation, so H goes to the CH2 end and Br adds to the carbon already bearing Br, giving the geminal dibromide CH3CHBr2.

items.stem: 1-Butyne (CH3CH2C#CH) is treated with 1.0 equivalent of NaNH2 in liquid ammonia at -33 degC. Which species predominates after deprotonation is complete?
choices: The neutral starting alkyne (no acid-base reaction)
A carbanion at the propargylic CH2
items.why: The terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25) is by far the most acidic site because the resulting acetylide anion has its lone pair in an sp orbital with 50% s-character, holding charge close to the nucleus. NaNH2 (conjugate acid NH3, pKa ~38) is more than strong enough to deprotonate it cleanly, generating the 1-butynide acetylide.

items.stem: 2-Butyne is hydrogenated using H2 over Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/CaCO3 poisoned with Pb and quinoline) in hexanes at room temperature. What is the geometry of the alkene product?
items.why: Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned Pd surface that delivers both hydrogens to the same face of the alkyne (syn addition) and is deactivated enough to stop at the alkene stage. Syn addition across the internal alkyne places the two methyls on the same face, giving the (Z) (cis) alkene.

items.stem: 1-Butyne is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 and a catalytic amount of HgSO4 at 60 degC. After tautomerization of the initially formed enol, what is the major isolated carbonyl product?
items.why: Hg(II)-catalyzed hydration of an alkyne is Markovnikov: water adds to the more substituted carbon (C2 of 1-butyne), giving the enol CH3CH2C(OH)=CH2. Keto-enol tautomerization always favors the carbonyl, so the enol shifts a proton to give the methyl ketone 2-butanone. Terminal alkynes always give methyl ketones under these conditions, never aldehydes.

items.stem: 2-Butyne is reduced with sodium metal dissolved in liquid ammonia at -78 degC (dissolving-metal reduction). What is the stereochemistry of the alkene product?
items.why: Na/NH3 reduces alkynes via single-electron transfers that produce a trans-vinyl radical anion intermediate, where the two substituents minimize steric strain by sitting on opposite faces. Anti protonation locks in that geometry, so dissolving-metal reduction is the standard way to make (E) (trans) alkenes from internal alkynes.

items.stem: 1-Butyne (pKa ~ 25) is treated with sodium amide (NaNH2, pKa of NH3 ~ 38) in dry THF at 0 degC. Which conjugate base is generated as the principal product?
choices: No deprotonation occurs (NaNH2 is too weak)
items.why: Comparing pKa values, NH3 (38) is far less acidic than the terminal alkyne C-H (25), so the equilibrium lies completely on the side of acetylide. The terminal C-H is acidic because the acetylide lone pair sits in an sp orbital (50% s-character), placing negative charge close to the nucleus and stabilizing the anion.

items.stem: Treatment of 1-butyne with 1.1 equivalents of NaNH2 in NH3(l) at -33 degC removes the most acidic proton. Which carbanion is generated, and on which carbon does the negative charge reside?
choices: An allyl anion delocalized over C1-C2-C3
No reaction; alkyne C-H bonds are not acidic
A terminal acetylide anion at C1 (sp carbon)
An sp3 carbanion at the C3 propargylic position
items.why: Acidity tracks s-character of the orbital holding the lone pair: sp (terminal alkyne C-H, pKa ~25) >> sp2 (vinyl, ~44) > sp3 (alkyl/propargyl, ~50). The terminal C1-H is by far the most acidic site, so NaNH2 selectively removes it to give the C1 acetylide; the propargylic CH2 protons are far less acidic and are not touched.

items.stem: 1-Butyne is subjected to acid-catalyzed hydration using H2O, dilute H2SO4, and a catalytic amount of HgSO4 at room temperature. Following Markovnikov addition and keto-enol tautomerization, what is the major product?
items.why: HgSO4/H2SO4 hydration of a terminal alkyne adds water in Markovnikov fashion, placing the OH on the internal (more substituted) carbon to give an enol. The enol then tautomerizes to the more stable keto form, and because OH ended up on C2, the carbonyl forms at C2, giving the methyl ketone 2-butanone.

items.stem: 1-Butyne is hydrated with dilute H2SO4 and HgSO4 in aqueous THF. The initially formed Markovnikov enol tautomerizes under the acidic conditions. Which carbonyl compound is isolated as the dominant product, and why is it favored over its tautomer?
choices: 2-butanone, because the more substituted enol gives the thermodynamically stable methyl ketone
2-butanol, from net Markovnikov hydration without oxidation
Butanal, from anti-Markovnikov hydration via hydroboration
But-2-en-2-ol, the kinetic enol that fails to tautomerize
items.why: Markovnikov addition of water to 1-butyne puts OH on C2 (the more substituted alkyne carbon) to give but-1-en-2-ol. Keto-enol equilibrium overwhelmingly favors the carbonyl because the C=O bond is much stronger than C=C plus O-H, so the enol tautomerizes to give the methyl ketone, 2-butanone.

items.stem: 2-Butyne is reduced using Na metal in liquid NH3 at -78 degC, proceeding through a trans-vinyl radical anion intermediate that protonates with anti geometry. What is the configuration of the resulting alkene?
choices: (E)-2-butene (trans), because the trans-vinyl anion is the stable intermediate
A 1:1 mixture of E and Z isomers
items.why: Dissolving-metal reduction (Na/NH3) generates a vinyl radical and then a vinyl anion intermediate; this anion adopts the trans configuration to minimize steric repulsion between the two substituents. Anti protonation preserves that geometry, giving the (E)-alkene as the only major product. This is the complementary partner to Lindlar's catalyst (which gives Z).

items.stem: Benzene is treated with concentrated HNO3 in concentrated H2SO4 at 50 degC. The H2SO4 protonates HNO3 to generate the active electrophile NO2+. What is the major product of this electrophilic aromatic substitution?
items.why: In nitration, H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and dehydrates it to nitronium ion (NO2+), the actual electrophile. Benzene's pi system attacks NO2+ to form a sigma-complex (Wheland intermediate), and loss of H+ restores aromaticity, giving nitrobenzene. The strong driving force to regain aromatic stabilization is why EAS substitutes rather than adds.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at room temperature. The Lewis acid activates Br2 toward attack by the aromatic pi system. What is the major monosubstituted product?
items.why: FeBr3 polarizes the Br-Br bond to generate a more electrophilic Br+ equivalent (Br-FeBr3 complex). Benzene attacks to form a sigma complex; loss of H+ rearomatizes the ring to give bromobenzene. Aromatic stability prevents addition products like dibromocyclohexane, and a single equivalent of Br2 stops at monosubstitution since bromine itself is deactivating.

items.stem: Benzene reacts with Br2 in the presence of a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 25 degC. Aromaticity is restored after loss of H+ from the Wheland (sigma) complex. What single product predominates?
items.why: EAS with Br2/FeBr3 follows the standard pathway: electrophilic attack by Br+, formation of a Wheland intermediate, and loss of H+ to restore aromaticity. The driving force is recovery of ~36 kcal/mol of aromatic stabilization, which is why substitution wins over addition. The result is bromobenzene; without light or peroxides, no radical side-chain bromination occurs.

items.stem: On a benzene ring already bearing -Cl, -Br, or -F, a halogen substituent has unusual electronic behavior in electrophilic aromatic substitution. Which combination of activating/deactivating effect and directing effect best describes a halogen substituent?
choices: Deactivating but ortho/para directing (sigma withdrawal vs. pi donation)
Neither activating nor deactivating; ipso directing only
items.why: Halogens are the textbook exception: they withdraw electron density inductively through the sigma bond (electronegativity), which slows EAS overall (deactivating). However, they can donate a lone pair into the ring through resonance, and that pi donation specifically stabilizes the sigma-complex from ortho/para attack, making them ortho/para directors despite being deactivators.

items.stem: Benzene is stirred with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 in CCl4 at room temperature. After workup, what is the major product of the electrophilic aromatic substitution?
items.why: FeBr3 acts as a Lewis acid catalyst that polarizes Br2 into a more electrophilic species (effectively Br+). Benzene's pi cloud attacks, forming a Wheland intermediate, and proton loss rearomatizes the ring to give bromobenzene. With only 1 equivalent of Br2 and bromine being weakly deactivating, the reaction stops at monosubstitution.

items.stem: Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires a relatively electron-rich aromatic ring to attack the carbocation electrophile. Which substrate fails to undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation under standard AlCl3/RX conditions?
choices: Strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene
items.why: Friedel-Crafts alkylation needs a sufficiently nucleophilic aromatic ring to attack the alkyl cation electrophile. Strong electron-withdrawing groups (-NO2, -CN, -SO3H, -COR) deplete pi density to the point that the ring cannot attack, and the carbocation electrophile reverts or polymerizes instead. Nitrobenzene is the classic 'won't-react' substrate for FC alkylation.

items.stem: Nitrobenzene is treated with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 80 degC. The -NO2 group is strongly deactivating and a meta director. What is the major monobromination product?
choices: No reaction occurs at any temperature
items.why: Drawing the resonance forms of the sigma complex shows that ortho and para attack place positive charge directly on the carbon bearing -NO2, which is severely destabilized by the electron-poor nitrogen. Meta attack avoids that conflict, so meta is the least bad option for a strong deactivator. Heat is required because the ring is deactivated, but meta is still the major regiochemistry, giving m-bromonitrobenzene.

items.stem: Benzene is nitrated with a 1:1 mixture of concentrated HNO3 and concentrated H2SO4 at 50 degC. The active electrophile generated in situ is the nitronium ion (NO2+). What is the major aromatic product?
items.why: H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and dehydrates it to NO2+, the nitronium ion electrophile. Benzene attacks NO2+, forms a Wheland intermediate, and loses H+ to rearomatize, giving nitrobenzene. The aromatic ring is preserved (so no nitrocyclohexane), and the nitro group strongly deactivates the ring against further nitration under these conditions.

items.stem: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, ortho/para-directing activators stabilize the sigma-complex by donating electron density into the ring. Which set lists only activating ortho/para directors?
items.why: Activating ortho/para directors are groups that donate electrons into the ring through pi resonance (-OH, -NH2, -OR, -NHR via lone pair donation) or through hyperconjugation/induction (alkyl groups). They stabilize the positive Wheland intermediate from ortho/para attack. Halogens are an exception (deactivating but o/p-directing), while -NO2, -COOH, and -CN are deactivating meta directors.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 in CH2Cl2 at room temperature with a catalytic amount of FeBr3 as the Lewis acid. Which product results from electrophilic aromatic substitution?
items.why: FeBr3 polarizes Br-Br to make Br+ more available; benzene's pi system attacks to form a sigma complex, which loses H+ to recover aromaticity. With only one equivalent of Br2 and bromine being a deactivator, monobromination dominates and gives bromobenzene. Polar (ionic) conditions in the dark suppress radical side-chain pathways.

items.stem: When benzene is combined with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 25 degC in the dark (to suppress radical chemistry), the reaction proceeds via a Wheland intermediate. What is the major product?
items.why: With FeBr3 as a Lewis acid in the dark, the polar EAS pathway dominates: Br+ adds to benzene to form a Wheland intermediate, then H+ departs to restore aromaticity, giving bromobenzene. Dark conditions exclude the radical pathway that would give benzyl bromide, and aromatic stabilization (~36 kcal/mol) ensures substitution rather than addition.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in the presence of a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 30 degC. Which product is consistent with electrophilic aromatic substitution under these polar conditions?
items.why: Br2 alone is too weakly electrophilic for benzene, but FeBr3 forms a Br-Br-FeBr3 complex with much greater Br+ character. Benzene attacks, the sigma complex loses H+, and aromaticity returns, giving bromobenzene. Polar/ionic conditions favor EAS over radical (no light/peroxides), and aromaticity prevents addition products like dibromocyclohexane.

items.stem: Nitrobenzene is brominated with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 100 degC. The -NO2 group withdraws electron density both inductively and through resonance. Where does bromination occur and what is the major product?
choices: No reaction; nitrobenzene is inert to EAS
items.why: Drawing the sigma-complex resonance structures for ortho or para attack on nitrobenzene puts a positive charge directly on the ring carbon bearing the strongly electron-withdrawing -NO2 group, which is severely destabilizing. Meta attack avoids that overlap, making meta the most stable (least bad) sigma complex. Heat overcomes the deactivation but the directing preference is maintained, giving m-bromonitrobenzene.

items.stem: Nitrobenzene reacts sluggishly with Br2/FeBr3 at elevated temperature. The strongly electron-withdrawing nitro group destabilizes the sigma-complex when ortho or para attack occurs. Which is the major monobromination product?
choices: An equal mix of o- and p-isomers
items.why: All meta-directing groups are deactivating because they pull electrons out of the ring; for -NO2, the resonance structures of ortho and para attack place positive charge adjacent to the electron-poor nitrogen, which is highly unstable. Meta attack puts the positive charge only on carbons not attached to -NO2, so it is the least destabilized pathway and gives m-bromonitrobenzene.

items.stem: Toluene is treated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 with catalytic FeBr3 at room temperature (polar, ionic conditions). Where does the methyl substituent steer electrophilic bromination?
choices: Benzyl bromide via radical side-chain bromination
items.why: Alkyl groups are weak activators and ortho/para directors because they donate electron density via hyperconjugation/induction to stabilize the positive sigma-complex when attack occurs ortho or para. Sterics make the para isomer the largest fraction with the ortho a smaller share; meta is disfavored. FeBr3 (polar conditions) ensures EAS rather than radical side-chain bromination.

items.stem: Friedel-Crafts alkylation uses an alkyl carbocation electrophile generated from RCl/AlCl3, which requires a sufficiently nucleophilic aromatic substrate. Which substrate is essentially unreactive under standard FC alkylation conditions?
choices: Strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene
items.why: Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires the ring to be at least as nucleophilic as benzene. Strongly deactivating groups (-NO2, -CN, -SO3H, -COR) drain enough pi density that the ring cannot effectively attack the alkyl cation, and the cation rearranges or polymerizes instead. Halobenzenes are deactivated but still react; nitrobenzene is the canonical 'fails FC alkylation' substrate.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in the presence of a catalytic amount of FeBr3. The mechanism involves attack on Br-FeBr3, formation of a sigma complex, and loss of H+ to restore aromaticity. What is the major product?
items.why: The mechanism is the textbook EAS: FeBr3 polarizes Br2 into a stronger Br+ source, the arene attacks to form a sigma (Wheland) complex, and loss of H+ regenerates aromaticity. Recovery of aromatic stabilization (~36 kcal/mol) makes substitution greatly preferred over addition, so the product is the flat aromatic bromobenzene.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with a 1:1 mixture of concentrated HNO3 and H2SO4 at 50 degC. Sulfuric acid protonates HNO3, which loses water to give NO2+. After electrophilic substitution and rearomatization, which product is isolated?
items.why: H2SO4 generates the nitronium ion (NO2+) by protonating and dehydrating HNO3. The arene attacks NO2+ to form the sigma complex, and proton loss restores aromaticity to give nitrobenzene. The newly installed -NO2 is strongly deactivating, so a second nitration would require much harsher conditions and would go meta.

items.stem: Benzene is brominated with Br2 (1.0 equiv) and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 in CH2Cl2 at room temperature. Although Br2 alone reacts only sluggishly with arenes, FeBr3 polarizes Br-Br to generate a stronger electrophile. What is the principal product?
items.why: Lewis acid activation by FeBr3 makes Br2 electrophilic enough for benzene to attack. The standard EAS pathway (sigma complex formation, then H+ loss) gives bromobenzene. Without a leaving group on the ring, no SNAr is possible; without light or peroxides, no radical side-chain bromination occurs.

items.stem: Benzene reacts with one equivalent of Br2 in the presence of FeBr3 to deliver Br+ to the aromatic ring. Loss of an aromatic H+ regenerates the catalyst and gives a flat, aromatic product. What is the major isolated species?
items.why: EAS substitutes (rather than adds) because the arene regains its ~36 kcal/mol aromatic stabilization upon proton loss. With only 1 equivalent of Br2, the reaction stops cleanly after one substitution, and the catalyst (FeBr3) is regenerated by deprotonation. The flat, aromatic product is bromobenzene.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with concentrated HNO3 in concentrated H2SO4 at approximately 50 degC. Once the nitronium ion (NO2+) attacks the aromatic ring and the sigma-complex loses H+, what is the major product?
items.why: Standard mixed-acid nitration produces NO2+ from HNO3 and H2SO4, which acts as the EAS electrophile on benzene. The sigma complex loses H+ to rearomatize, yielding nitrobenzene. The strongly deactivating -NO2 group prevents over-nitration under these conditions, so dinitration requires forcing conditions.

items.stem: Nitrobenzene is brominated with Br2/FeBr3 at 130 degC. Resonance structures of the sigma-complex show that ortho and para attack place positive charge on the ring carbon bearing the electron-poor -NO2 group, which is destabilizing. Which product dominates?
choices: No reaction (the ring is fully deactivated)
items.why: When the question explicitly walks you through the resonance argument, it's telling you why -NO2 is a meta director: ortho/para attack leads to a sigma-complex where positive charge sits on the carbon bearing -NO2 (destabilizing). Meta attack avoids that conflict, making it the least bad pathway. Heat overcomes the deactivation, but selectivity stays meta, giving m-bromonitrobenzene.

items.stem: Toluene is brominated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 in CH2Cl2 at room temperature (no light, no peroxides). Which regiochemistry results from electrophilic aromatic substitution on the methyl-substituted ring?
choices: Benzyl bromide via radical side-chain bromination
items.why: The methyl group is a weak activator and ortho/para director: it donates electron density via hyperconjugation/induction, stabilizing the sigma-complex when the new group ends up ortho or para. Sterics give a larger para fraction than ortho. FeBr3 + dark conditions select EAS over radical side-chain (NBS or Br2/light), so the ring brominates rather than the methyl group.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 25 degC in CH2Cl2. The reaction proceeds through formation of a sigma-complex (Wheland intermediate) and loss of an aromatic H+. What is the major product?
items.why: FeBr3 activates Br2 toward electrophilic attack; benzene's pi cloud forms a sigma complex with Br+, then H+ departs to restore aromaticity. Substitution rather than addition is the outcome because the arene regains its aromatic stabilization. With only 1 equivalent and -Br being deactivating, monobromination dominates, giving bromobenzene.

items.stem: Benzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with concentrated HNO3 in concentrated H2SO4 at 50 degC. The H2SO4 functions as both Bronsted acid and dehydrating agent to generate the nitronium ion (NO2+). What is the major product?
items.why: Under mixed-acid conditions, H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and removes water to generate NO2+, the electrophile. Benzene attacks NO2+ to form the sigma-complex, which loses H+ to restore aromaticity, yielding nitrobenzene. The aromatic ring stays intact (preventing nitrocyclohexane), and there is no oxidation pathway here to give benzoic acid.

items.stem: Halogens (-Cl, -Br, -F) on benzene exhibit competing electronic effects: strong sigma withdrawal versus weak pi donation from a lone pair. How does this combination manifest in electrophilic aromatic substitution?
items.why: The two effects act on different things: inductive sigma withdrawal slows the overall reaction (deactivating), but pi donation of a halogen lone pair specifically stabilizes the sigma complex of ortho/para attack through resonance, beating out meta attack. The net result is that halogens are deactivating but ortho/para directing, the only group class with this combination.

items.stem: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is treated with NaOMe in methanol at room temperature (basic conditions). Where does the methoxide nucleophile attack the epoxide carbons?
choices: The less-substituted (less hindered) carbon, via SN2
No reaction; epoxides are inert to alkoxides
Exclusively the oxygen, giving an O-methylated species
items.why: Under basic (no acid) conditions, the epoxide oxygen is not protonated and ring opening is governed by sterics in a clean SN2: the nucleophile attacks the less-substituted, less-hindered carbon from the back side. There is no carbocation character, so the more-substituted carbon (electronically more polarized in acid) is not preferred.

items.stem: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is opened with HBr in CH2Cl2 at 0 degC. The acid first protonates the epoxide oxygen, and bromide then attacks one of the ring carbons. Where does Br- end up?
choices: On the more-substituted carbon (acid-catalyzed, partial carbocation character)
On the oxygen, giving an alkyl hypobromite
items.why: Under acidic conditions, HBr protonates the epoxide oxygen first, weakening the C-O bonds. The more-substituted carbon develops partial carbocation character (tertiary > secondary > primary) and stretches its C-O bond more, which makes it the better electrophile despite being more hindered. Br- attacks there, giving Markovnikov-like regiochemistry, opposite to base-mediated opening.

items.stem: 1-Propanol is treated with Jones reagent (CrO3 in dilute aqueous H2SO4 with acetone as cosolvent) at 0 degC, with excess oxidant. What is the major isolated product after workup?
items.why: Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4/H2O/acetone) is a wet, strongly oxidizing chromium reagent. The aqueous acid hydrates the initial aldehyde to a gem-diol, which is then re-oxidized to the carboxylic acid. Primary alcohols thus go all the way to the carboxylic acid (propanoic acid here); to stop at the aldehyde, you need an anhydrous reagent like PCC.

items.stem: 1-Propanol is oxidized using excess Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4 in aqueous acetone) at room temperature for 1 hour. Aqueous strong-oxidant conditions over-oxidize primary alcohols past the aldehyde stage. What is the major product?
items.why: Jones reagent contains water, which hydrates the propanal intermediate to a gem-diol; CrO3 then re-oxidizes that gem-diol to the carboxylic acid. Because the over-oxidation step is fast under aqueous acid, the reaction does not stop at the aldehyde stage and goes all the way to propanoic acid.

items.stem: 1-Propanol is stirred with excess Jones reagent (CrO3, H2SO4, aqueous acetone) at 0 degC. The water present hydrates any aldehyde intermediate to a gem-diol, which is then oxidized further. What is the major final product?
items.why: The stem walks through the mechanism: water hydrates propanal to a gem-diol, and the gem-diol's C-H is then oxidized again by CrO3 to give the carboxylic acid. This is why aqueous chromium oxidants (like Jones) take primary alcohols to carboxylic acids rather than stopping at aldehydes; PCC, by contrast, has no water and stops at the aldehyde.

items.stem: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is opened by NaOMe in dry methanol at 25 degC under basic conditions. Without acid to polarize the C-O bonds, the regiochemistry is governed by sterics. Which site does methoxide attack?
choices: The less-substituted (less hindered) carbon via SN2
The oxygen atom, generating an oxocarbenium ion
items.why: In neutral or basic epoxide opening, there is no protonation to generate carbocation character, so the reaction is a textbook SN2 on the less-hindered ring carbon. The methoxide approaches from the back side opposite the oxygen, displacing it as an alkoxide. Steric (not electronic) factors dominate.

items.stem: Under basic conditions, sodium methoxide opens 2,2-dimethyloxirane (isobutylene oxide) in MeOH at room temperature. With no protonation of the epoxide oxygen, regiochemistry is dictated by steric accessibility. Where does MeO- attack?
choices: On the oxygen, giving an O-methylated zwitterion
items.why: Without acid catalysis, the epoxide oxygen is a relatively poor leaving group and the reaction is a normal SN2: the nucleophile attacks the less-hindered carbon. In 2,2-dimethyloxirane, that is the CH2 end, since the geminal-dimethyl carbon is too crowded for backside attack.

items.stem: The Williamson ether synthesis couples an alkoxide with an alkyl halide via SN2. To minimize competing E2 elimination from a hindered substrate, which combination of starting materials is preferred?
items.why: The Williamson ether synthesis is an SN2 reaction, so the alkyl halide should be primary (or methyl) to allow clean backside attack with minimal steric blocking. Using a tertiary alkyl halide instead leads almost exclusively to E2 elimination because the alkoxide is also a strong base. Pairing a primary halide with the alkoxide gives the highest ether yield.

items.stem: tert-Butanol is heated with concentrated H2SO4 at 80 degC. The protonated alcohol loses water to give a stable tertiary carbocation, which then undergoes E1 elimination. What is the major organic product?
items.why: With concentrated H2SO4 and heat, tertiary alcohols undergo E1 dehydration: protonation of OH gives water as the leaving group, ionization yields a stable tertiary carbocation, then a beta-proton is lost to give the alkene. From tert-butanol, the only alkene possible is isobutylene (2-methylpropene).

items.stem: 1-Propanol is treated with Jones reagent (CrO3 in dilute H2SO4, aqueous acetone) at room temperature with the alcohol added dropwise. The aqueous acid hydrates the initially formed aldehyde, which is then re-oxidized. What is isolated?
items.why: Jones is an aqueous chromium oxidant: water hydrates the propanal intermediate to a gem-diol, and CrO3 re-oxidizes the C-H of the diol to give propanoic acid. This is the standard way to take a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; an anhydrous reagent (PCC) would be needed to stop at the aldehyde.

items.stem: tert-Butanol is heated to 100 degC in concentrated H2SO4. After protonation and loss of water, the tertiary carbocation eliminates a beta-proton via E1. What is the major product of this acid-catalyzed dehydration?
items.why: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of tertiary alcohols proceeds through an E1 mechanism: H2SO4 protonates the OH, water leaves to give a tertiary carbocation (which is stable), and a beta-proton is removed by the conjugate base. From the symmetric tert-butyl cation, only one alkene is possible: isobutylene (2-methylpropene).

items.stem: When designing a Williamson ether synthesis to make a methyl alkyl ether, the alkyl halide should be the less hindered partner so that SN2 outcompetes E2. Which combination is best?
choices: Aldehyde + alcohol, with no acid catalyst
Aryl bromide + sodium ethoxide in ethanol
items.why: The Williamson ether synthesis is an SN2 reaction, so steric crowding kills it: tertiary halides give E2 elimination instead. The optimal pairing places the alkyl group on the halide side as primary (or methyl) and the bulkier group on the alkoxide. Aryl halides don't work either because SN2 doesn't proceed on sp2 aromatic carbon.

items.stem: 1-Propanol is stirred with excess Jones reagent (CrO3, H2SO4, aqueous acetone) at room temperature for 1 hour. Because water is present, any propanal intermediate is hydrated and oxidized again. What is isolated?
items.why: The mechanism of over-oxidation: water hydrates propanal to its gem-diol form, and CrO3 then oxidizes the gem-diol's C-H to a second C=O, giving the carboxylic acid. So aqueous chromium oxidations (Jones, K2Cr2O7) take primary alcohols all the way to carboxylic acids; here, propanoic acid.

items.stem: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is opened with HBr in ether at 0 degC. The acid protonates the oxygen, lengthening the C-O bond at the more-substituted carbon to give partial carbocation character. Where does Br- attack?
items.why: Acid catalysis flips epoxide regiochemistry compared to basic conditions. After protonation, the more-substituted carbon develops more positive (carbocation-like) character because tertiary > secondary > primary carbocation stability, and its C-O bond stretches. Br- therefore attacks the more-substituted carbon despite the steric hindrance, giving Markovnikov-like addition.

items.stem: The Williamson ether synthesis is a classic backside SN2 displacement of a halide by an alkoxide. To synthesize a target ether without significant elimination byproducts, which substrate-nucleophile pair is preferred?
items.why: SN2 requires backside attack on a relatively unhindered electrophilic carbon. A primary alkyl halide is ideal because there is little steric blocking and the alkoxide (a strong base) won't have time to abstract a beta-proton (E2). Tertiary halides give E2 instead, and vinyl/aryl halides don't undergo SN2 at all.

items.stem: tert-Butanol is heated to 80 degC with concentrated H2SO4. After protonation of the hydroxyl, water leaves to give a tertiary carbocation that loses a beta-proton in an E1 step. What is the principal product?
items.why: Tertiary alcohols dehydrate easily under H2SO4 because the intermediate carbocation is well-stabilized. From tert-butanol, deprotonation of any of the equivalent CH3 beta-positions on the tert-butyl cation gives the same alkene: isobutylene (2-methylpropene). 1-butene cannot form because the carbon skeleton lacks a CH2-CH3 chain.

items.stem: In a Williamson ether synthesis, the SN2 displacement of halide by alkoxide is the most common scheme. To avoid significant E2 elimination from the bulky alkoxide, which combination of partners is best?
choices: Tertiary alkyl halide + alcohol with H+
items.why: Alkoxides are strong bases as well as nucleophiles, so any time the alkyl halide is hindered (secondary or tertiary), E2 elimination dominates. Picking a primary halide and putting the bulkier piece on the alkoxide side ensures clean SN2 because the primary carbon is sterically open for backside attack.

items.stem: A target ether is to be made by Williamson ether synthesis. SN2 backside attack on the alkyl halide by the alkoxide must outpace E2 elimination, so steric crowding on the electrophile must be minimized. Which combination is preferred?
choices: Aryl chloride + sodium methoxide in methanol
items.why: The competition between SN2 (gives ether) and E2 (gives alkene) is decided by sterics on the electrophile: bulkier halides shift the balance toward elimination. A primary alkyl halide minimizes that crowding, letting SN2 win cleanly. Aryl halides cannot undergo SN2 because the sp2 carbon and ring geometry block backside attack.

items.stem: 2-Propanol is treated with PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in CH2Cl2 at 25 degC, or alternatively with Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4) at 0 degC. A secondary alcohol cannot be over-oxidized because it lacks an alpha-hydrogen-bearing carbonyl carbon. What is the product?
items.why: Secondary alcohols give ketones on oxidation, and the reaction stops there because the resulting ketone has no C-H on the carbonyl carbon for further oxidation. Both PCC (anhydrous) and Jones reagent (aqueous) thus produce the same ketone from 2-propanol, namely acetone. Only primary alcohols differ between PCC (stops at aldehyde) and Jones (over-oxidizes to acid).

items.stem: When planning a Williamson ether synthesis, choose the alkyl halide and alkoxide so that SN2 occurs cleanly on a sterically uncluttered carbon. Which combination is preferred when forming an unsymmetrical ether?
items.why: Always assign the alkyl halide to the less hindered partner because SN2 needs backside access to the electrophilic carbon. Primary halides allow clean substitution; tertiary halides give E2 elimination; and vinyl/aryl halides simply don't undergo SN2 because their sp2 carbons can't accept backside attack.
